title: The Dentist Who Invented Forensic Identification
event_summary: On May 4, 1897, a catastrophic fire at the Bazar de la Charité in Paris killed 126 people, mostly aristocratic women, burning them beyond visual recognition. Cuban-born dentist Oscar Amoedo systematically identified the dead by matching their dental records to their remains, publishing his landmark work 'L'Art Dentaire en Médecine Légale' the following year. This was the first large-scale, scientifically documented use of forensic odontology to identify disaster victims.
why_forgotten: The fire itself was sensationalized for its class dimensions—wealthy women dying at a charity bazaar—overshadowing Amoedo's methodological breakthrough. His Cuban origins and the fact that dentistry was considered a lesser medical discipline meant his contribution was rarely credited in broader histories of forensic science. European forensic narratives later emphasized fingerprinting and DNA, retroactively minimizing earlier identification techniques.
why_it_matters: Amoedo's protocols became the foundation for modern mass disaster victim identification, used after events from the 9/11 attacks to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Every forensic odontology textbook traces the discipline's origins to his Paris work. His framework established the principle that scientific identification of the dead is a civic obligation, shaping international disaster response protocols still used by Interpol today.
